newsitem.title: CHINA: China says something for all in HK. Can it deliver?.
newsitem.headline: China says something for all in HK. Can it deliver?.

text.p: China's President Jiang Zemin promised something for everyone on Tuesday, the first day of his rule over an expanded realm, vowing communist fingers would not meddle in Hong Kong's capitalist pie.

But analysts said communist influences surfaced in Hong Kong within hours of Beijing's resumption of sovereignty and wondered whether China's rulers could realise Jiang's pledge that "water from the well will not intrude into water from the river".

Speaking to Hong Kong at the end of his whirlwind visit to receive back from Britain China's Special Administrative Region, Jiang offered guarantees of continued prosperity and greater democracy to its 6.4 million people.
"No central department or locality may or will be allowed to interfere in the affairs which... should be administered by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region on its own," Jiang promised.

A few hours earlier and almost without time to draw breath after the solemn handover, Jiang presided at the swearing-in of a new Beijing-anointed legislature -- a ceremony that proceeded with all the stilted formality of Chinese communist events.
"The swearing-in was very interesting," said one Asian diplomat in Beijing. "It was very redolent of the way they do things up here."

To round off the occasion, the band in the glittering harbourfront Convention Centre played the song "I love Beijing's Tiananmen" that traditionally closes many Communist Party and government meetings in the cavernous Great Hall of the People overlooking Tiananmen Square.
Much of Jiang's speech was aimed at reassuring those who doubt communist China will keep the promises made by late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping not to change capitalist Hong Kong for 50 years.

"These policies and guidelines have been formulated by the Central People's Government after careful consideration of the need to safeguard both the immediate interests of the Hong Kong compatriots and the fundamental interests of the Chinese nation," Jiang said.
"Therefore, there is no reason whatsoever to change them," he said, adding that Deng's 50-year pledge was firm. "This is a long-term basic principle of ours."
"It is clearly business as usual," the Asian diplomat said.

Jiang's speech was a monument to conciliation, promising gradual democracy, a directly-elected chief executive -- eventually -- and even offering a word of thanks to the British imperialists who withdrew from this southern corner of the Chinese empire after an occupation of 156 years.
"They're going ahead with this pretty much as you would expect," said another diplomat.

"The Chinese leaders are making all the right noises, the entry of the troops was completely according to plan," he said, referring to the orderly convoys of 4,000 People's Liberation Army soldiers and sailors who swept in shortly after dawn, waving with white-gloved hands.
But other analysts say that dramas almost certainly lie ahead.

"The eyes of the world are on them today," said one Western sinologist. "But what happens after the spotlight moves away from Hong Kong? What happens if things start to go wrong? The communists have one way of handling themselves.
